---
title: Figmint tracks artifact provenance
author: Example Author
---

A small document whose figures carry their own provenance. They were produced by
scripts figmint knows nothing about; what figmint knows is what each script was
given, what environment it ran in, and what came out.

## The figure

::: {.figmint src="figures/composite.svg" #fig-performance width="95%"}
**(a)** Power coefficient and **(b)** torque coefficient against tip speed
ratio, measured in a towing tank—synthetic values for this example.
:::

Expand the panel under [@fig-performance] and you get what a reader would
otherwise have to take on trust: what this picture was made from, whether it is
still current, and—where the record says so—which parts were made with a
generative tool. All of it is read from `figmint.toml` and the files' own
Content Credentials when the document builds. Nothing on this page is typed by
hand.

That is a *composite*: two panels, arranged in draw.io, exported as one SVG.
Its chain is three deep and the panel above lists all of it, because "what was
this made from" is not answered by naming the diagram it came out of.

## The same figure, interactive

A figure need not be a picture. Point the block at an HTML file and it is
embedded in a frame, numbered and cross-referenced like any other—hover for the
numbers, drag to zoom, double-click to reset:

::: {.figmint src="figures/cp_curve_interactive.html" #fig-cp height="400px"}
Power coefficient against tip speed ratio, drawn by Plotly as a web page rather
than an image—the same measurements as panel (a) of [@fig-performance].
:::

Its panel is amber, and deliberately so. Every hash behind [@fig-cp] matches —
nothing is stale, nothing was tampered with, every automated check passes — and
the script that drew it is a file nobody has claimed. That is the gap this tool
exists to make visible, and it is the easiest one in the world to miss, because
nothing is *failing*. Left as a green tick with the finding folded away inside
the panel, figmint would be the one doing the hiding.

It is a warning rather than an error because nothing is broken and no output
needs regenerating. What is missing is a person's statement, and only a person
can supply it:

```sh
figmint declare scripts/plot_cp_interactive.py --mine --with-ai 'Claude Opus 5'
```

Run that and the panel goes green. It is left undone here on purpose, so the
state is visible in a built document rather than only described in a README.

This is also where the record earns the most. [@fig-cp] **cannot carry Content
Credentials at all**: c2pa does not recognize HTML in either direction, so
there is nowhere in the file for a manifest to live. The panel underneath it is
the only provenance this figure has, which is exactly why the warning at the
top of `figmint.toml` is not decoration.

The file is self-contained—Plotly's library is inlined rather than fetched from
a CDN—and that is a provenance decision rather than a convenience one. An
artifact that downloads half of itself at read time is not an artifact anybody
can hash: what a reader sees would depend on what that URL served them, and
figmint would be recording the wrapper rather than the figure. It costs a few
megabytes, which is the honest price.

The static panels are a different trade. `figures/cp_curve.svg` is an SVG,
which *can* carry Content Credentials, so it is signed where it is made and the
disclosure survives into the composite instead of stopping at the first
re-encode.

## How it got there

```sh
figmint run -i data/performance.csv -o figures/cp_curve.svg \
    -- pixi run python scripts/plot_cp.py
```

figmint hashed the inputs, ran the command, hashed the output, and recorded all
of it. It did not read the script, and it does not need to.

figmint also recorded `scripts/plot_cp.py`, which was never passed with `-i`.
Any file the command names is hashed too—forgetting the script is the easiest
mistake to make and among the worst to live with, since it is the input most
likely to change and its omission would leave the figure looking current after
the code that drew it was rewritten.

### The environment is an input

The command has to go through a manager with a deterministic lock file—here
`pixi run`, so `pixi.lock` is recorded alongside the CSV. That is not
bookkeeping. The same script under a different Plotly draws a different figure,
and a record naming only the data would call that unchanged.

pixi rather than uv, and for a reason this document is the proof of: **Quarto
is in that lock too**. Rendering this page is a recorded step, so figmint
records `pixi.lock` as its environment—and if Quarto came from a system install
the lock would be asserting an environment it does not actually pin. The record
would be claiming more than it knows, which is the one thing it must never do.
A different Quarto renders a different page, exactly as a different Plotly draws
a different figure.

### Going stale

```sh
make break     # edits the data
figmint status # the figure is now out of date
```

The check compares the hash of every recorded input against the file on disk.
There is no cache to invalidate and no timestamp to be confused by; either the
bytes match what was recorded or they do not.

::: {.callout-warning}
`figmint status` reporting a figure as stale means the figure is stale. The fix
is to regenerate it—never to edit the hashes in `figmint.toml`. That file is
evidence, and a record edited to match files it does not describe is
indistinguishable from a forged one.
:::

## How the composite was assembled

A figure made of several panels is an artifact whose inputs happen to be other
artifacts:

```sh
figmint drawio import figures/cp_curve.svg figures/composite.drawio
figmint drawio import figures/ct_curve.svg figures/composite.drawio
# ...arrange it in draw.io...
figmint drawio export figures/composite.drawio figures/composite.svg
```

Each panel goes in byte-for-byte, carrying `src` and `hash` on its shape, and
the diagram is recorded with the panels as inputs. Regenerating a panel makes
the composite stale—which nothing inside draw.io could ever notice, since it
holds a *copy* with no link back.

Use the figmint command rather than draw.io's own **Insert → Image**. draw.io
re-encodes anything over 1200 px through a canvas before embedding it, which
destroys whatever Content Credentials the image carried.

`import` is an *authoring* step: it puts a new panel on the canvas, and you
should not need to run it again when a panel is redrawn. You don't—each shape
records where it came from, so `drawio export` re-embeds any panel that has
moved on, keeps the position and size you gave it, and says which ones it
touched. That is why `figures/composite.drawio` is committed here while
everything else under `figures/` is generated: the *arrangement* is the work.

### Why export is a separate step

A `.drawio` is a source; it is not a picture anything but draw.io can display.
`figmint drawio export` renders one, and does three things while it is there:

- exports with `--embed-diagram`, so the shapes' `src` and `hash` survive into
  the SVG and the published file can still be checked;
- **re-records the diagram**, because editing it in draw.io is the entire point
  of keeping one and every edit changes its bytes. Without this the composite
  would sit permanently `modified`, and that signal—*somebody wrote this file
  behind figmint's back*—would be worth nothing;
- signs the result, naming both the diagram and its panels as ingredients.

## The data behind it

The block is not only for figures. Point it at a CSV and it renders the numbers
as a table, numbered and cross-referenceable like any other, with the same
provenance panel underneath—and this is where the record earns the most,
because a CSV cannot carry Content Credentials at all. For
`data/performance.csv` the line in `figmint.toml` is the *only* provenance
there is.

::: {.figmint src="data/performance.csv" #tbl-performance}
The measurements underlying [@fig-performance].
:::

The eleven points in [@tbl-performance] are the whole dataset.

## The whole document

A document is a composite too—of every artifact it embeds. The graph is the
record itself, drawn: `figmint.toml` is already a DAG, so nothing here can
disagree with the freshness reported beside it.

::: {.figmint artifact="_site/index.html" table="true" graph="true"}
:::

Read it left to right and you have the answer to "where did this figure come
from": one CSV is read by two scripts, running under the environment the lock
file pins, to make two panels; the panels make the diagram; the diagram makes
the published picture; that makes the page. The scripts sit *in* the chain
rather than beside it, because that is what happened—a figure is not the sum of
a dataset, a lock and some code stirred together. Rounded nodes are raw inputs;
nothing in the project produced them.

figmint never reads the script, so that edge is inferred from the data and the
code having been inputs to the same command. It is the claim the record was
already making, drawn the way a reader traces it.

Two kinds of circularity had to be kept out of the way. `figmint.toml` is
deliberately *not* an input of the document, even though this filter reads it
to draw the panels above—recording the file that `figmint run` itself writes
would make the document stale the instant it finished building.

The subtler one is that a document cannot honestly report on its *own*
freshness from inside itself. While this page is being written the hash in the
record still describes the previous build, so the panel above would call itself
out of date on every render—permanently, and in the one place nobody can act
on it. That is what the `artifact=` option is for: it names this document's
output so the panel can show how to rebuild it and leave it out of its own
tally. `figmint status` checks it from outside, where the answer has settled.

## Where the chain ends

Follow any figure back far enough and you reach a file figmint did not make.
Here that is `data/performance.csv`—measurements—and the two plotting scripts.
`figmint run` cannot record where those came from, because figmint was not
there.

Left alone they are the hole in the middle of an otherwise checkable record: a
figure that is current in every link, resting on data nobody can place. Every
check above them passes, which is what makes the gap easy to miss. So a primary
artifact is *declared*, and the declaration says which kind of claim it is:

```sh
figmint declare data/performance.csv --mine
figmint declare scripts/plot_cp.py --mine --with-ai 'Claude Opus 5'
figmint declare scripts/plot_ct.py --mine --with-ai 'Claude Opus 5'
figmint declare figures/composite.drawio --mine
```

The `.drawio` is in that list because it is assembled from recorded panels but
*arranged* by hand. It has a derivation chain and an author list at the same
time, and declaring the authors leaves its inputs untouched.

`--mine` is an attestation—nothing verifies it, and figmint says so wherever it
is displayed. A DOI resolves to something a reader can fetch; `--git` and
`--calkit` name a location pinned to a revision.

Scripts count too, and so does generative AI. A model can produce a file but it
cannot answer for one, so a tool is named *alongside* an accountable person
rather than instead of one. A `.py` file has nowhere to put a manifest, so the
record is the only place that disclosure can live, and the panel says *per the
record*.

## Live preview

`quarto preview` re-renders when *its own* sources change—this file,
`_quarto.yml`, the images it links. A change to `scripts/plot_cp.py` is
invisible to it, so the panels above would keep showing the state from the last
render even though the figure had gone stale.

`make preview` closes that gap by watching everything figmint records as an
input and touching this file when any of it moves, which is the one thing
Quarto does notice. Edit the plotting script with the preview open and the
panels go red on their own.

One caveat, and it is the one people hit first. VS Code's Quarto extension
starts its preview with `--no-watch-inputs`, which turns off re-rendering on
file changes entirely—the extension re-renders when you *save this document*
and at no other time. Under that preview nothing on disk can make the panels
update, including the touch above. Run `make preview` in a terminal, or save
this file after editing a script.

When they do, `figmint rebuild` puts it right: the record knows the command
behind every artifact and the order they depend on each other in, so it runs
the repair sequence rather than printing it for you to retype.

The HTML is recorded but **not signed**: c2pa does not recognize the type at
all, so the page you are reading cannot carry a manifest under any tool. For
those outputs `figmint.toml` is the only provenance there is, which is exactly
why the warning at the top of it is not decoration.
